noteBlocks.text: Biological molecules and the energy in food

noteBlocks.md: Everything you eat is built from three kinds of molecule: carbohydrate, protein and fat, each a chain of smaller units. Some your body burns, some it stores, some it builds into cells. In the lab you burn a crisp and measure its energy.

noteBlocks.prompt: Fats and oils are made of glycerol and ______ ______ .
noteBlocks.explain: Fatty acids. Three of them attached to one glycerol — the pair of words is worth a mark each in a two-mark part.

noteBlocks.md:
**Carbohydrates.** The **simple** ones are sugars: **glucose** and **lactose**. They are an energy source and can be stored. The **complex** ones are long chains of sugar units: **starch** (storage in plants), **glycogen** (storage in animals) and **cellulose** (structural — it is what the plant cell wall is made of).
**Proteins** are chains of **amino acids** and are the **structural and functional** molecules of cells.
**Fats and lipids**, including oils, are **fatty acids and glycerol**, used as an energy source and for storage.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is a complex carbohydrate used for storage in animals?
noteBlocks.explain: Glycogen. Cellulose is structural and in plants; lactose is a simple sugar.

noteBlocks.title: Storage or structural?
noteBlocks.md:
**Storage:** starch (plants), glycogen (animals), fats and oils.
**Structural:** cellulose (plant cell walls) and proteins (in cells).
March 2026's Higher paper asked for exactly this split and most candidates could not give it. Two words, six molecules — learn it as a sorting job, not a sentence.

noteBlocks.caption: Burn a known mass of food under a known mass of water, and measure the rise.

noteBlocks.md: **The method.** Measure 20 cm³ of water into a boiling tube — 20 cm³ of water has a mass of **20 g**. Take the starting temperature. Weigh the food sample, set it alight in a Bunsen flame and hold it under the tube until it stops burning. Stir, and take the highest temperature reached. The **rise** is what you use.

noteBlocks.prompt: 20 cm³ of water has what mass, in g?
noteBlocks.explain: 20 g. One cm³ of water has a mass of one gram.

noteBlocks.title: The two lines of working
noteBlocks.md:
**energy transferred (J) = mass of water (g) × 4.2 × temperature rise (°C)**
**energy per gram (J/g) = energy transferred ÷ mass of food burned (g)**
The first mass is the **water**, never the food. The food's mass only appears in the second line. Papers print the 4.2 for you; they do not print which mass goes where.

noteBlocks.prompt: 20 g of water rises by 19 °C. The energy transferred, in joules, is
noteBlocks.explain: 20 × 4.2 × 19 = 1596 J. Do the multiplication in one line on the calculator rather than rounding halfway.

noteBlocks.md: **Then divide by the mass of food.** If that 1596 J came from burning **0.40 g** of crisp, the energy content is 1596 ÷ 0.40 = **3990 J/g**. Dividing by a number below one makes the answer bigger, which is a useful check: a small crumb releasing 1596 J means a whole gram would release far more.

noteBlocks.title: Why the mass in the first line is the water
noteBlocks.md: The 4.2 is the energy needed to warm **one gram of water by one degree**, so the mass beside it can only be the mass of **water**. The food's mass belongs in the second line.

noteBlocks.prompt: 1596 J came from burning 0.40 g of food. The energy content, in J/g, is
noteBlocks.explain: 1596 ÷ 0.40 = 3990 J/g. If your answer came out smaller than 1596 you divided the wrong way round.

noteBlocks.md: **Burn more, and the water gets hotter in proportion.** Repeat the burn with 0.2 g, 0.4 g, 0.6 g, 0.8 g and 1.0 g of the same cereal and the temperature rise climbs in step. Plotted, the points lie on a straight line **through the origin** — and that is the one shape that lets you write **directly proportional**. A straight line that misses the origin, or a curve, is 'related but not proportional'.

noteBlocks.title: March 2026 B1 Foundation Q2, March 2026 B1 Higher Q4(c), Summer 2024 Booklet A Biology
noteBlocks.md: In March 2026 the energy calculation itself was answered well — candidates used the formula they were given. What they could not do was the biology around it: another simple carbohydrate, what fat is broken down into, and whether each large molecule is structural or storage. In the practical units, the recurring arithmetic fault is typing an average as A + B ÷ 2 on the calculator, which does the division first. **Check that a mean sits between the two values.**

noteBlocks.prompt: Two results are 4.0 and 6.0 kJ. Give the mean, in kJ.
noteBlocks.explain: 5.0 kJ. A mean must sit between the two readings.

noteBlocks.md: **Why the answer is always too low.** Most of the energy released never reaches the water: it heats the air, the tube and the clamp, and some of the food does not burn completely. So the measured value is **lower than the true value** — an accuracy problem, not a reliability one. Shielding the tube from draughts, holding the food closer and using a lid all raise the measured value towards the truth. Repeating the burn and taking a mean does something different: it improves **reliability**.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student repeats the burn three times and takes a mean. What has she improved?
noteBlocks.explain: Repeats and agreement are reliability. Accuracy would need less energy lost to the surroundings; validity would need only one variable changed.

items.stem: In energy = mass × 4.2 × temperature rise, which mass is used?

items.stem: Why is the measured energy content of a food always lower than the true value?

options.text: Much of the energy heats the air, the tube and the clamp instead of the water

parts.workedSolution: temperature rise = 50 − 18 = 32 °C; energy transferred = 25 × 4.2 × 32 = 3360 J; energy per gram = 3360 ÷ 0.50 = 6720 J/g

The mass of food has been used in the energy line: 0.50 × 4.2 × 32 = 67.2 J. The water is what is being heated, so 25 g goes in there; the food's mass is only used in the second line. This is also only the energy line: the question asks for energy per gram of food.

context.setting: A student asked to compare the energy in a crisp with the energy in a piece of pasta

parts.stem:
A student wants to find out whether a crisp or a piece of dried pasta contains more energy per gram.
Describe how she should carry out the investigation so that her comparison is fair, and how she would work out the energy per gram.
Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: measure the same volume of water, for example 20 cm³, into a boiling tube each time
weigh each food sample and record its mass
take the starting temperature of the water with a thermometer
set the food alight and hold it under the tube on a mounted needle until it stops burning
stir, then record the highest temperature and find the rise
energy transferred = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature rise, then divide by the mass of food
keep the volume of water and the distance from the tube the same for both foods, and repeat each one

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: A fair comparison needs the same water, the same distance and the same method for both foods.
Finish with the two lines of calculation — the energy, then the energy per gram.
parts.workedSolution: Measure 20 cm³ of water into a boiling tube and clamp it. Weigh the crisp on a balance and record its mass. Take the starting temperature of the water with a thermometer. Hold the crisp on a mounted needle, set it alight in a Bunsen flame and hold it just under the tube until it stops burning. Stir the water and record the highest temperature, then work out the rise. Repeat everything with the pasta, using the same volume of water and the same distance from the tube. For each food, energy transferred = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature rise, and then energy per gram = energy transferred ÷ mass of food burned. Repeat each food three times and take a mean before comparing.

commonErrors.feedback: The energy line uses the mass of water. The mass of food only comes in at the end, when the energy is divided to give the energy per gram.

findTheMistake.stem:
Rónán is asked: 'A 0.60 g piece of biscuit was burned under 20 cm³ of water. The temperature rose from 19 °C to 45 °C. Calculate the energy content of the biscuit in J/g. (energy transferred = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature rise) [4]'
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The mass of food has been used where the mass of water belongs. The water is what is being heated, so 20 cm³ of water, which has a mass of 20 g, goes into the energy line. The 0.60 g is only used afterwards, to turn joules into joules per gram.
findTheMistake.feedback: The first line is right and earns its mark: the rise, not the final temperature. After that the wrong mass runs through everything, although the last line shows the right idea — divide by the mass of food — so the method is sound. A quick sense check catches it: 109 J/g would make a whole biscuit worth about as much energy as a spoonful of water warmed by a couple of degrees. Label the two masses on the page before you start: water for heating, food for dividing.

prompts.prompt: What are carbohydrates, fats and proteins each made from?
prompts.answer: Carbohydrates: sugar units such as glucose. Fats and oils: fatty acids and glycerol. Proteins: amino acids.

prompts.prompt: Storage or structural? starch ___, glycogen ___, cellulose ___, protein ___
prompts.answer: starch storage; glycogen storage; cellulose structural; protein structural (and functional).

prompts.prompt: Name the two simple carbohydrates on this specification, and their use.
prompts.answer: Glucose and lactose, used as a source of energy and for storage.

prompts.prompt: Write the two lines of working for the energy content of a food.
prompts.answer: energy transferred (J) = mass of water (g) × 4.2 × temperature rise (°C); energy per gram (J/g) = energy transferred ÷ mass of food burned (g).
keyWords: divide by the mass of food

prompts.prompt: In the energy equation, which mass is used — the food or the water?
prompts.answer: The water. The water is what is being heated. The mass of food is used only in the second line, to find the energy per gram.

prompts.prompt: Why is the measured energy content always too low, and what would improve it?
prompts.answer: Energy is lost to the air, the tube and the clamp, and some food does not burn completely. A draught shield, insulation or holding the food closer would make it more accurate. Repeating improves reliability, not accuracy.
